extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and literate readers interested in poetic composition and literary judgment (Romantic-era circles)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative commentary and practical aesthetic advice on poems and poetic composition, delivered as private/public letters between contemporary poets and critics. Focuses on originality, phrasing, meter, emotional effect, and critical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality of catastrophe/conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Joanna's ruin is a catastrophe too trite; and this is not the first or second time you have clothed your indignation, in verse, in a tale of ruined innocence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using stock or over-familiar climaxes; vary circumstances of the conclusion to make the catastrophe feel fresh (example suggestion: replace the gentleman seducer with a clumsy rustic country fellow such as a Roger-Lothario).

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture-work and circumstantial richness
rubrics_metrics.description: "It pleases me mightily, being so full of picture-work and circumstances."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems that supply vivid pictures and concrete circumstances win approval; include strong, particular imagery and incident work to ground emotion and scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-invention and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion that a "Roger-Lothario" (a novel, rustic seducer) would be a fresh character to explore.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer inventive character-types over conventional archetypes; novel characterization can renew familiar themes and avoid cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Felicity of phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: "It has no felicity of phrase, no old-fashioned phrase or feeling."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek felicitous, striking turns of phrase; loss of felicitous diction weakens poetic effect—look for phrases that feel right and memorable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter/measure: novelty and appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The measure, too, is novel and pleasing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive or pleasing measures (rhythm, cadence) are a virtue; meter that feels fresh and fitting to subject-matter enhances a poem's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terseness and subtle pathos ('more felt than strikes the ear')
rubrics_metrics.description: "A terseness, a jocular pathos which makes one feel in laughter... where more is felt than strikes the ear."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economy and understated poignancy are desirable—poems that imply feeling rather than over-explaining it produce stronger emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of quality across stanzas/sections
rubrics_metrics.description: "The fourth stanza is less striking, as being less original. The fifth falls off."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain sustained quality; later stanzas should not drop in originality or felicity—revise to ensure evenness across the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of modern sentimental clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: "'Young hopes, and love's delightful dreams,' savor neither of Burns nor Quarles; they seem more like shreds of many a modern sentimental sonnet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of shopworn sentimental phrases that drain individuality; prefer idiom and imagery that avoid blending into generic sentimentality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity of feeling (avoid imposed tracks of feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is sometimes revolting to be put in a track of feeling by other people, not one's own immediate thoughts."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor genuine, personally-derived emotion over contrived or conventional affect; readers resent being led into prescribed emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter novelty: using animals/lowly subjects to open sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: "I love this sort of poems, that open a new intercourse with the most despised of the animal and insect race... A series of such poems... would take excessively."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploring neglected or despised subjects (rats, toads, cockchafers, worms, etc.) can be both novel and morally useful—such choice of subject can rescue creatures from antipathy and open new emotional registers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review practice: extract and cite elaborate beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: "You have selected a passage fertile in unmeaning miracles, but have passed by fifty passages as miraculous as the miracles they celebrate. I never so deeply felt the pathetic as in that part... You should have extracted 'em.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reviewing, present and quote the most elaborate or beautiful passages rather than ignoring them; reviewers should acknowledge and exhibit notable strengths, not only faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of epithets and public praise
rubrics_metrics.description: "For God's sake... don't make me ridiculous any more by terming me gentle-hearted in print... the meaning of 'gentle' is equivocal at best, and almost always means 'poor-spirited.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious with laudatory epithets—public praise can misrepresent a person's character; choose descriptors that cannot be misread or used to ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude of voice and image for character
rubrics_metrics.description: "Witches illustrate, as fine ladies do, from their own familiar objects, and snakes and shutting up of wombs are in their way."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a character's imagery, metaphors, and actions consistent with their persona and everyday referents—details should feel natural to the speaker's world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of decisive editorial cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: "I perfectly accede to all your alterations, and only desire that you had cut deeper, when your hand was in."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong, even ruthless, editorial pruning can improve a piece; don't be shy to cut more deeply to sharpen effect and remove flab.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical authority requires adequate reading/preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical project criticized for grand claims without reading: George intends broad judgments on drama and epic despite not having read many primary authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make sweeping critical claims without reading the relevant primary works; authority in criticism depends on acquaintance with texts one critiques or compares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware mechanical observance of 'laws of verse' (rhyme spacing as ostentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: "George writes odes where the rhymes, like fashionable man and wife, keep a comfortable distance of six or eight lines apart, and calls that 'observing the laws of verse'... George tells you, before he recites, that you must listen with great attention, or you'll miss the rhymes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skepticism toward mechanical rule-following: don't treat formal devices (like far-spaced rhyme) as ornaments that demand artificial attention; form should serve content and not be theatrical pedantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composing a tragedy as a deliberate medley of modes
rubrics_metrics.description: "My tragedy will be a medley... of laughter and tears, prose and verse, and in some places rhyme, songs, wit, pathos, humor, and if possible, sublimity..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A deliberate mixing of modes (comic and tragic, prose and verse, songs and sublimity) can be an intentional artistic choice—if aiming for a medley, balance the discordant colors so they serve the whole.
